title: The last stakes
hook: the brothers are staked one by one, then Yudhishthira himself, then Draupadi, and the oldest Hindu scripture already warned against it
carry: the rig veda: play not with dice

segments.voice: Yesterday, stake after stake, the drumbeat of I have won, and Vidura's man reaching for honey. Where dharma is, there is victory.

Every treasure is gone. In the telling, Yudhishthira stakes his herds, his lands, his city, even the ornaments the princes wear. Lost, every one. And then the game changes from a matter of things to a matter of people. Shakuni asks: is there anything left? There is. Sitting near Yudhishthira, listening to all of it, are his four brothers.
screen: `EVERY TREASURE IS GONE.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING LEFT?` → `HIS FOUR BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira stakes Nakula, one of the twins. Shakuni wins. He stakes Sahadeva. Lost. Then Shakuni tries something sly: the twins are Madri's sons; surely Kunti's sons, Bhima and Arjuna, are dearer to you. An attempt to split the brothers. Yudhishthira catches it: you're trying to divide us, and that's wrong. Then, as if to prove they can't be divided, he stakes Arjuna. Lost. Bhima. Lost. Himself. Lost. Shakuni says one stake is left: Draupadi. And Yudhishthira stakes her. The elders break into a sweat. Vidura holds his head in his hands. The blind king keeps asking whether the throw is won. Shakuni throws, and wins. Now the teaching. Hindu scripture saw this coming long before the epic. In the Rig Veda, the oldest Hindu scripture, there's a hymn in the voice of a gambler. He says the dice pull at him like a drink he cannot refuse; his wife, who never wronged him, pushes him away; his own family won't know him. And the hymn ends, in effect: play not with dice; till your field. That's why Hindu law books count dice among the vices, not the pastimes: not because a game is wicked, but because the dice ask for more and more, until the stakes are people. Yudhishthira's loyalty to his brothers was real, and the dice took that too. For today: anything that keeps asking you to stake a little more, an app, a bet, a habit, is the hymn's dice. Plough your field instead.
screen: `THE TWINS, ONE AFTER THE OTHER.` · `ARJUNA, BHIMA, HIMSELF, DRAUPADI.` · `THE RIG VEDA'S GAMBLER.` · `DICE: A VICE, NOT A PASTIME.` · then, large: `PLAY NOT WITH DICE; TILL YOUR FIELD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you'd stand up for without thinking, a sibling, a friend, a partner, a child, and let their faces come one at a time. Hold each one simply, on no table, part of no bet, breathing in with one face and out with the next. If you pray, you can hold each of them in your prayer; if not, simply wish each of them well.
Pana, a wager. Brothers are staked one by one, a king loses himself, and Draupadi is lost in a game she never played.
Your line: the Rig Veda says, play not with dice. Tomorrow, the one who was staked asks a question. Day seven hundred sixty-nine, done.

howItsDone: The last stakes of the dice game are read aloud and staged as a turning point of the epic, and many Hindu teachers set them beside the Rig Veda's gambler's hymn as a warning about the dice.

Pana.meaning: a wager, a stake laid down in a game

Nakula.meaning: one of the twin Pandavas, a son of Madri

Madri.meaning: Pandu's second wife, mother of the twins

Kunti.meaning: mother of Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna

Draupadi.meaning: the princess married to the five Pandava brothers

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (the final stakes: herds, lands, city, ornaments; Nakula, Sahadeva, Arjuna, Bhima, Yudhishthira himself, Draupadi; Shakuni's taunt about Madri's and Kunti's sons; the elders' distress; Dhritarashtra asking whether the stake was won)
Rig Veda 10.34, the gambler's hymn (Akshasukta): the gambler's lament for his wife and family; closing advice not to play with dice but to till the field
Manusmriti 7.47 (dice among the vices born of desire, listed for kings)
